hints: Focus on what excess $H_2$ with Ni does to each $C=C$ bond, it adds two H atoms and turns $C=C$ into $CH-CH$.
Spot the three $C(CH_3)=CH$ groups in P, after hydrogenation each $C(CH_3)$ becomes $CH(CH_3)$, a strong candidate for chirality.
Test every saturated carbon for four different groups, remembering that $CH_2$, $C(CH_3)_2$ and $C= C$ carbons can never be chiral.
walkthrough:
**Understand the hydrogenation**

Think of this as simply filling up all the double bonds with hydrogen. Each $C=C$ becomes $CH-CH$.

$$C=C + H_2 \xrightarrow{Ni} CH-CH$$

**Count the double bonds in P**

Look carefully at compound P. It has three trisubstituted alkene units, each of the type $C(CH_3)=CH$.

After full hydrogenation, product Q has no $C=C$ left. It is fully saturated, so every ring carbon is now $CH_2$, $CH$ or $C$.

**Recall the test for chiral**

A chiral carbon must be $sp^3$, bonded to four different groups, so it is usually $CH$ connected to three different carbon chains, or $CH(CH_3)$ in different environments.

$CH_2$ groups have two H atoms, so never chiral. $C(CH_3)_2$ has two identical methyls, so never chiral.

**Count chiral centres in Q**

First, the three former $C(CH_3)=$ carbons each become $CH(CH_3)$. Because they sit in different positions of the large fused ring system, left and right chains are different, so all three are chiral. That gives 3.

Next, look at the ring junction and bridge region. The gem-dimethyl $C(CH_3)_2$ itself is not chiral, but the two saturated bridgehead $CH$ carbons next to it are each joined to four different ring segments, so both are chiral. That adds 2 more.

All other carbons are $CH_2$ groups and are achiral. Total is $3 + 2 = 5$ chiral carbon atoms.

options.A: 4 is one too few. Students choosing this often count the three new $CH(CH_3)$ centres correctly but miss one of the ring junction $CH$ centres near the gem-dimethyl bridge.
options.B: 5 is correct. The three hydrogenated $C(CH_3)$ carbons become chiral $CH(CH_3)$ centres, plus two chiral saturated ring-junction $CH$ carbons, while $CH_2$ and $C(CH_3)_2$ carbons are achiral.
options.C: 6 is one too many. This comes from incorrectly counting the quaternary $C(CH_3)_2$ carbon as chiral, but it has two identical methyl groups so it cannot have four different groups.
options.D: 7 is too high. This comes from counting $CH_2$ carbons or alkene $CH$ carbons in P as chiral, forgetting that chiral carbons must be saturated and have no duplicate H atoms or duplicate methyls.
